questions_and_answers.question: If a waiter/waitress doesn't leave your check on the table, how can you ask for it?
What does the word '(o)kanjoo' literally mean?
Where can you pay the check, depending on the restaurant?

answers.answer: Either to a waiter/waitress or to the cashier

questions_and_answers.question: If you're not sure where to pay, what can you ask?

answers.answer: Okanjoo wa doko desu ka? (Where do I pay?)

questions_and_answers.question: If you can pay the waiter/waitress directly, what will s/he say?
If you are supposed to pay the cashier, what will the waiter/waitress say?

answers.answer: Achira desu. / Achira de onegai shimasu. (Over there. / Pay over there, please.)

questions_and_answers.question: What word for 'cashier' (from 'register') may be used instead of 'achira'?

answers.answer: reji (as in Reji de onegai shimasu)

questions_and_answers.question: When you leave, what will the cashier or waiter/waitress probably say?

answers.answer: Maido/doomo arigatoo gozaimashita. Mata doozo. (Thank you very much. Please come again.)

questions_and_answers.question: What expression can you use to say you enjoyed the meal?
Is it necessary to say you enjoyed the meal?

answers.answer: No, it isn't necessary (just as in a shopping situation), but Japanese people often do
No, and it is considered rude to say it

articles.text:
4. Paying the check and leaving the restaurant

If a waiter/waitress doesn't leave your check on the table, you can ask for it by saying:

Okanjoo onegai shimasu.    Check, please.

The word (o)kanjoo literally means 'calculation.' Thus, the above sentence literally means 'Please calculate (how much I owe you OR how much I should pay).'

Depending on the restaurant, you can pay the check either to a waiter/waitress or to the cashier. If you are not sure, ask a waiter/waitress by saying:

Okanjoo wa doko desu ka?    Where do I pay?

If you can pay the waiter/waitress directly, s/he will say something like the following:

Koko/kochira de onegai shimasu.    Here, please.

S/he then will take the money to the cashier and bring back your change, if any. If you are supposed to pay the cashier, s/he will say something like:

Achira desu.                  Over there.
Achira de onegai shimasu.     (Pay) over there, please.

She may use the word reji 'cashier' (from 'register') instead of achira as in the following:

Reji de onegai shimasu.    (Pay at) the cashier, please.

When you leave, the cashier or the waiter/waitress will probably say:

Maido/doomo arigatoo gozaimashita.    Thank you very much.
Mata doozo.                            Please come again.

Although it isn't necessary for you to say anything (just as in a shopping situation), Japanese people often say that they enjoyed the meal. If you want to do the same, you can use the following expression:

Gochisoosama (deshita).    I've enjoyed the meal.
